title: The decoy effect: the middle option that steers you
description: Two prices become three, and suddenly the expensive one looks sensible. Shops add a deliberately unattractive option not to sell it, but to move you — here is how to spot the trap.

body.heading: The option nobody is meant to buy
paragraphs: The classic demonstration is a subscription sold in three forms: online-only for one price, print-only for a much higher price, and print-plus-online for that same higher price. The print-only option is a decoy — dominated by the bundle at the same price — and its presence makes the bundle look like obvious value, dramatically increasing how many people choose it.
Remove the decoy and most people pick the cheap option. Nothing about the two real choices changed; only the company they kept.

body.heading: How to shop past it
paragraphs: When you see three tiers, cover the middle one — literally, with a thumb — and compare the remaining two on their own merits: what do you get, what does it cost, what would you pay for that difference elsewhere?
Then ask the decoy question: which option here exists only to make another look good? Naming the decoy out loud breaks most of its power, in shops, software pricing pages and coffee sizes alike.

takeaway: A decoy option exists to make a pricier choice look like value. Cover the middle tier and compare the other two on their own merits.
